Who Improves the Robot? Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement

Hai Zhou, Fan Yang, Zeyi Chen, Lejun Zhang, Chenyang Fu, Jianping Li, Jiayi Zhu, Xianyang Liu, Yingxuan Yang, Lili Meng, Lu Wang, Xinyang Han, Jiankai Sun, Weirui Ye, Guanchu Wang, Wanhua Li, Ming Zhou, Boyi Li, Ming Jin, Kun Shao, Muhao Chen, Guang Chen, Lei Ma, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Costas Spanos, Xia Hu, Mac Schwager, Weinan Zhang, Qian Feng, Shangding Gu Shanghai Jiao Tong University Google   Microsoft University of California, Berkeley Stanford University Massachusetts Institute of Technology Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory Nanyang Technological University Nvidia   Virginia Tech   Xiaomi University of California, Davis Tongji University University of Tokyo Singapore Management University Technical University of Munich
Abstract

Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting updates to both a robot’s capabilities and its improvement procedure, making subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. We present an L0–L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substantial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priorities in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/Physical-RSI.

Keywords: Recursive Self-Improvement, Physical Artificial Intelligence, Agentic Systems, Robot Learning.

Contents

1 Introduction

Advances in robotics have enabled machines to carry out an expanding range of tasks on their own, from sorting parcels in logistics centers to performing routine chores at home (Zeng et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2025). Yet behind this execution autonomy lies a reliance on human support. In data preparation, robots do not have data as abundant as the internet data available to language models. Their data is generated through thousands of physical interactions, and humans are needed to collect and review it (Collaboration et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024). In deployment, when a robot meets an unfamiliar failure, recovery largely depends on humans to diagnose the problem or demonstrate a fix (Liu et al., 2023b). In training and optimization, most systems rely on training pipelines designed by humans, and the final choice of which update to adopt remains a human decision (Zhu et al., 2020a). Consequently, even highly capable robots lack improvement autonomy, meaning the ability to improve themselves without humans driving the loop.

Recent work has begun to narrow this gap by letting systems improve themselves. One line of work lets language model agents rewrite code or scaffolding, and keep the changes that score better under automated evaluation (Zelikman et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026d; Novikov et al., 2025). Another line improves the model itself, training it on data and feedback that the system or another language model generates (Yuan et al., 2024b; Zweiger et al., 2025; Ghasemipour et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024d). Most of this work achieves self-improvement, in that the system raises its own task performance by changing what it uses when it performs a task. The procedure that produces and selects these changes usually stays fixed, so what the system can gain is limited by how effective that procedure is. Recursive self-improvement goes further. It updates the improvement procedure itself. Recursive gain is established when the revised procedure produces better subsequent improvements than its predecessor under matched conditions. Few works however update the procedure, and fewer show that doing so yields recursive gain.

Moreover, recursive self-improvement is harder for robots in the real world than in simulated or digital environments. The physical world cannot be monitored as exhaustively as digital environments. A robot observes only partial and noisy traces of what actually happened, which makes failures hard to diagnose and improvements hard to verify (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2019). Outcomes are also less deterministic than in digital environments, and the robot must act through continuous dynamics under real-time constraints (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2019). Evaluating any change therefore requires repeated trials under noisy conditions, which is time-consuming on real robots (Zhou et al., 2025b). Finally, resetting a physical system is expensive, hardware can fail, and many interactions risk irreversible outcomes, including harm to people who share the workspace, so the cheap trial and error on which self-improvement in digital environments relies becomes costly and risky (Eysenbach et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020a). These constraints make it particularly hard on real robots to update and to verify the changes. Physical robots therefore call for a recursive self-improvement framework of their own, rather than one carried over from digital settings.

We build this framework around Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI). We say that a robot performs Physical RSI when it uses evidence from its physical interaction to persistently update both its task-execution system and its improvement procedure, such that its subsequent improvement becomes more effective over successive rounds. Here the task-execution system is the models and harness that the robot uses to perform tasks, and the improvement procedure is the part that can update the task-execution system and itself. An independent evaluator assesses the gains of the updated system. Our long-term vision is for robots to operate and evolve autonomously in real-world physical environments, addressing diverse and unforeseen challenges without human intervention.

Based on this definition, we introduce six levels, L0 to L5, to describe how much of it a system meets, as shown in Figure 1. L0 covers systems that make no retained change on their own, either because they adjust only within a run or because humans still drive the loop. L1 to L4 vary along two axes. Capability-level updates change the task-execution system, whereas meta-level updates change the improvement procedure. The second axis is scope. A gain on a single task may be specific to that task, whereas a gain across multiple tasks shows that the update generalizes. L1 makes capability-level updates on a single task with the improvement procedure fixed, and L2 adds meta-level updates on the same task. L3 and L4 extend L1 and L2, respectively, to multiple tasks. L5 builds on L4 and requires evidence, from an independent evaluator under the same controlled conditions, that each update yields a larger gain than the previous one. The formal definition and the detailed criteria are given in Section 2.

Existing surveys cover complementary parts of this framework. Surveys centered on components and experience examine how agents change their models, prompts, memory, tools, and workflows (Gao et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026a). RSI-oriented accounts ask whether the mechanisms that generate, evaluate, and select updates can themselves change (Liu et al., 2026c; Duan et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026b), and address safety through governance, independent evaluation, and the preservation of safeguards across updates (Liu et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026b; Gong et al., 2026). For humanoids, Nguyen et al. (2026) formulate admissible evolution through layered safety mechanisms. Such safeguards carry more weight in the physical world, where a failed trial cannot simply be rerun or rolled back (Duan et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026). We therefore make safety and control explicit in our system framework and dedicate a section to how they constrain physical interaction and autonomous improvement. And existing accounts characterize the scope of improvement in different ways. Liu et al. (2026c) reserve a higher level for broad transfer, Wang et al. (2026b) treat transfer as a separate empirical question, and Wu et al. (2026b) separately record improvement targets and held-out transfer while cautioning against collapsing independent dimensions into a single autonomy ladder. For robots, generalization remains uneven across changes in objects, embodiment, and deployment conditions (Hou et al., 2026b). We therefore cross two criteria in L0–L5, namely, whether an update changes the task-execution system or the improvement procedure, and whether its demonstrated effects remain within one task or extend across tasks. Finally, the task-execution system and the improvement procedure play different roles, but both involve models, harnesses, and associated improvement procedures (Liu et al., 2026c; Ren et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026b). We therefore organize methods into harness adaptation and model learning. This groups methods that operate on similar components while preserving the distinction between what the robot can do and how it improves.

This study makes three contributions. First, we propose Physical RSI as a concept and give it a graded framework from L0 to L5. The framework treats what is updated and how far an update reaches as orthogonal criteria to define L1–L4. Second, we investigate existing methods along two implementation paths, harness adaptation and model learning, each covering both the task-execution system and the improvement procedure, together with the safety and control mechanisms that bound both, and the verification that decides which updates are kept. Third, we review how existing systems are evaluated, set out a protocol for independently evaluating improvement procedures, and identify the evidence gaps that separate current work from higher levels.

The remainder of the study is organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the framework, including the definition, the system architecture, the L0–L5 levels, and the boundaries of evidence. Section 3 surveys harness adaptation, and Section 4 surveys model learning. Section 5 addresses safety and control, and Section 6 examines how Physical RSI is evaluated. Section 7 discusses open problems, and Section 8 concludes.

2 Foundations of Physical Recursive Self-Improvement

This section establishes the foundations for analyzing Physical RSI. Section 2.1 defines the system components and the conditions for physical self-improvement and Physical RSI, and relates them to neighboring research paradigms. Section 2.2 describes the execution, capability-level update, and meta-level update loops. Section 2.3 specifies task identity and the criteria for assigning levels L0–L5. This framework also provides a shared terminology for the analysis throughout the study.

2.1 Definition and Scope of Physical RSI

We describe an improving robot by its task-execution system and improvement procedure (Figure 1(a)), together with two properties of its updates, physical grounding and inheritance.

Task-execution system

The task-execution system is the pipeline through which the robot turns a task into action. It has two parts. The harness HH comprises the components outside the learned models, such as prompts, memory, skills and tools, task decomposition and recovery logic, and interface and controller code. The parametric models are the learned models used during execution, such as a planner, a vision-language-action policy, or a value function or world model, and we denote their weights by Θ\Theta. Capability can reside in either part, so we track both. Anything used only in the improvement procedure and not during task execution belongs to Φ\Phi rather than to the task-execution system (Section 2.3).

Improvement procedure

The improvement procedure Φ\Phi is responsible for improving the whole system, including the task-execution system and the procedure itself. It has three stages. An adaptation stage 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} updates HH. A training stage 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} selects experience and optimizes Θ\Theta. A verification stage 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} judges each candidate change proposed by 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} or 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} and decides whether to keep it. Φ\Phi can also improve itself by changing these stages, with an update to 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} or 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} judged by 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} and an update to 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} judged by the independent evaluator EE introduced below. This matters because an improvement procedure is designed around particular tasks. When new tasks arrive, a fixed procedure usually has to be re-engineered by people, whereas one that can update itself adapts without them. We call changes to the task-execution system capability-level updates and changes to the improvement procedure meta-level updates, and Section 2.2 describes how each is carried out.

Physical grounding

The improvement procedure draws its changes from experience, which it keeps in an experience and feedback store DD. DD stores the records of task execution, together with the records of improvement. Memory in HH holds what 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} has distilled from DD for use in HH. Experience may come from the real world, from a physics simulator, from a learned world model, from humans, or from signals inside the system. Among these sources, only the real world shows how the robot’s actions actually play out. A physics simulator reproduces contact and dynamics only approximately. A learned world model, humans, or internal signals can propose candidates or supply additional data, but a change drawn only from them is not physically grounded. We therefore call a change physically grounded when it depends on what happened as the robot acted, either in the real world or in a physics simulator.

Inheritance

A change becomes the starting point of later behavior only if it is inherited. We call the state retained after kk rounds of execution and improvement the kk-th generation 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k},

𝒮k=(Θk,Hk,Φk,Dk),Φk=(𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍k,𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇k,𝖵𝖾𝗋k),\mathcal{S}_{k}=(\Theta_{k},\ H_{k},\ \Phi_{k},\ D_{k}),\qquad\Phi_{k}=(\mathsf{Adapt}_{k},\ \mathsf{Train}_{k},\ \mathsf{Ver}_{k}), (1)

in which Θk\Theta_{k} and HkH_{k} form the task-execution system, 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍k\mathsf{Adapt}_{k}, 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇k\mathsf{Train}_{k}, and 𝖵𝖾𝗋k\mathsf{Ver}_{k} form the improvement procedure, and DkD_{k} is the experience and feedback store. Processes outside the robot, such as a training server or a language-model agent that edits code, belong to the system when a stage of Φ\Phi invokes them and they write into 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}. In round k+1k+1, generation kk executes tasks, its trajectories are added to DkD_{k} to give Dk+1D_{k+1}, and the improvement procedure Φk\Phi_{k}, applied as the map defined by its three stages, produces the next generation,

(Θk+1,Hk+1,Φk+1)=Φk​(Θk,Hk,Φk,Dk+1).(\Theta_{k+1},H_{k+1},\Phi_{k+1})=\Phi_{k}\left(\Theta_{k},H_{k},\Phi_{k};\,D_{k+1}\right). (2)

The initial generation 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} is the state at the start of the period over which improvement is claimed. A change is inherited when Φ\Phi keeps it on evidence in DD and it persists beyond the episode in which it was made, so that later generations start from it unless a later update changes it. Since Φk\Phi_{k} is one of its own arguments in Eq. (2), an inherited change may reach the improvement procedure, including 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} itself. A change to 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} cannot be judged by 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} alone, which is why the framework also needs a judge EE outside Φ\Phi.

Verification and evaluation

𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} and the independent evaluator EE both judge changes, but they stand in different positions and serve different purposes. 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} is a stage of Φ\Phi. It acts within every round, deciding which candidate changes proposed by 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} or 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} are kept, and because it belongs to Φ\Phi, it can itself be changed. EE is a set of tasks with a scoring criterion QQ that Φ\Phi cannot read, train on, or modify, and it stands outside the system. It has two roles. It judges changes to 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver}, since a 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} that judged its own changes could learn to satisfy its own standard without becoming better. It also scores the task-execution system (Θk,Hk)(\Theta_{k},H_{k}) once an update is complete, because it is this part that acts on the environment, while the improvement procedure is evaluated indirectly, by scoring the systems it produces. We write JQ​(Θk,Hk)J_{Q}(\Theta_{k},H_{k}) for the score of generation kk on EE under QQ. EE is extended from outside the system as it meets new tasks. Once EE is extended, earlier scores no longer measure the same thing, so earlier generations are either re-evaluated on the updated EE or compared on an anchor subset held fixed throughout the comparison. Section 6 describes how EE is built and used.

Definitions

Building on the task-execution system, the improvement procedure, physical grounding, inheritance, and the independent evaluator, we now define two notions of self-improvement. Definition 1 asks whether the robot has become better through changes that it made and kept on its own, and Definition 2 asks, more strictly, whether the way it becomes better has also become better.

Definition 1 (Physical self-improvement).

A system performs physical self-improvement over rounds 1,…,K1,\dots,K if the following conditions hold.

  1. (i)

    Capability-level self-inheritance. At least one change to Θ\Theta or HH is produced by stages of Φ\Phi and inherited. Changes to Φ\Phi may also be inherited but are not required. No human writes into Θ\Theta, HH, or Φ\Phi.

  2. (ii)

    Physical grounding. The inherited changes on which the retained gain depends are physically grounded, whether in a physics simulator or in the real world.

  3. (iii)

    Retained gain. JQ​(ΘK,HK)>JQ​(Θ0,H0)J_{Q}(\Theta_{K},H_{K})>J_{Q}(\Theta_{0},H_{0}).

Definition 2 (Physical recursive self-improvement).

Physical self-improvement is recursive if the following conditions hold, where (i) and (iii) strengthen the corresponding conditions of Definition 1.

  1. (i)

    Meta-level self-inheritance. In addition to condition (i) of Definition 1, Φ\Phi is able to update its own stages, so that changes to Φ\Phi produced by Φ\Phi can be inherited and used by later rounds.

  2. (ii)

    Physical grounding. The inherited changes on which the gain depends are physically grounded, whether in a physics simulator or in the real world.

  3. (iii)

    Recursive gain across tasks. Starting from the same generation and experience, and under the same budget, the system produced by each updated Φk\Phi_{k} scores a higher JQJ_{Q} than the system produced by Φk−1\Phi_{k-1}, with the gain measured across tasks.

Relation to continual learning, AutoML, and RSI

Table 1 compares the two definitions with three neighboring lines of work. Continual learning updates Θ\Theta from a sequence of tasks while limiting forgetting (Parisi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024b), including on robots (Lesort et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2026b), and so supplies the retention that physical self-improvement requires. Its task sequence and update rule are fixed by the designer, however, so Φ\Phi does not change. Automated machine learning searches over pipeline, model and training configurations for each problem (Hutter et al., 2019; He et al., 2021), which in our terms is mostly a search over the settings of 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train}. Some systems meta-learn from earlier problems to warm-start later searches (Feurer et al., 2022), which updates the procedure in part, but the system found for one problem is not carried over to the next, so changes are not inherited. General RSI frameworks describe an agent by its foundation model, harness, data system, trainer, and improvement mechanism (Liu et al., 2026c), which map onto Θ\Theta, HH, DD, and Φ\Phi, and allow all of them to change (Tang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026d). Such frameworks, however, mostly consider digital environments and do not require changes to be physically grounded.

Physical RSI requires real-world grounding, which separates it from RSI in digital environments in four ways.

  1. 1.

    Continuous, real-time interaction. The robot acts through continuous dynamics under real-time constraints, and a task counts as done only when it is completed physically, whereas digital environments can often be paused and replayed.

  2. 2.

    Costly and irreversible trials. Resets are expensive and some actions cannot be undone, whereas a digital environment can be restored to an earlier state.

  3. 3.

    Partial, noisy observation. The robot sees only local, noisy traces of what happened, whereas digital environments can often expose the full state. Outcomes are therefore uncertain, failures are hard to attribute, and evidence from simulation does not fully carry over to the real robot (the sim-to-real gap).

  4. 4.

    Safety of people and hardware. Robots often work alongside people, and the hardware itself can fail or be damaged, so safety constraints, and human oversight where people are involved, need to bound the loops.

These differences are also why our framework requires physical grounding for Physical RSI.

2.2 System Architecture and Improvement Loops

Section 2.1 defined the elements of an improving robot. This section shows how they work together within a round of Eq. (2). A round runs three loops that differ in what they change (Figure 2(a)), as Table 2 summarizes.

Three loops

In the execution loop, the task-execution system uses HH and Θ\Theta to turn observations and the episode context into actions, and adds the trajectory to DD. Behavior that improves within an episode, for example through replanning, ends with the episode and is not evidence of improvement.

In the capability-level update loop, Φ\Phi reads DD and changes HH and Θ\Theta, the parts the robot uses when it executes tasks. 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} may turn a successful trajectory into a reusable skill or store a lesson from a failure in memory, and 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} may fine-tune a policy on its own successful trajectories or update a world model with observed transitions. The changes that 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} accepts are inherited, so their effect shows on later tasks, where EE measures the gain (Section 2.1).

In the meta-level update loop, Φ\Phi changes one of its own stages, which the robot does not use while executing tasks but which produces or judges its later changes. An updated 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} may learn, for instance, to locate the failing module before rewriting a prompt. An updated 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} may switch from imitation learning to reinforcement learning with a reward derived from real outcomes when imitation stops improving a skill. An updated 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} applies a different standard for accepting candidates, such as other tests, success checks, or thresholds. 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} can accept an update to 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} or 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} by trying the updated stage and judging the changes it produces, whereas an update to 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} is judged by EE.

Two pathways: HH with 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt}, Θ\Theta with 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train}

Updates follow two pathways, each pairing a part of the task-execution system with the stage of Φ\Phi that updates it. The harness pathway pairs HH with 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} and is reviewed in Section 3, and the training pathway pairs Θ\Theta with 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{Train} and is reviewed in Section 4. Both run through the capability level and the meta level. The pathways interact. Skills and recovery routines added to HH change which trajectories enter DD for training, and an updated Θ\Theta changes which harness edits are worth proposing. Updates to 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} lie on neither pathway and are covered under evaluation (Section 6).

Feedback and safety

Feedback is the information that reaches later updates through DD. It comes from task execution, which supplies outcomes, internal signals, and human corrections, and from updates, which leave a record of what was changed and how 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} or EE judged it. Errors in feedback travel the same route. A misdetected success can lead 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} to accept a harmful change, and a misattributed failure can send 𝖠𝖽𝖺𝗉𝗍\mathsf{Adapt} to edit the wrong module. For safety, it constrains all three loops rather than being checked once after training, because physical trials can be irreversible and robots often share space with people (Section 2.1). During execution, action filters and human takeover keep trials safe, and 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} rejects updates that violate safety requirements or degrade earlier capability. Since an updated 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} might relax these tests, the safety rules are kept out of reach of Φ\Phi and, together with EE, form the protected constraints (Section 5).

2.3 The L0–L5 Framework

Figure 1(b) and Section 1 introduced the levels. This section states when a workflow meets each of them. The answer depends on what is changed, what counts as a task, and how far the gain extends beyond it. Figure 2 illustrates the update targets and the distinction between same-task and across-task evaluation.

Where a component sits

We assign each component to HH, Θ\Theta, or Φ\Phi by whether the task-execution system uses it. A component used to carry out a task belongs to HH or Θ\Theta. LRLL (Tziafas and Kasaei, 2024) keeps a library of executable skills that the policy code calls during task execution, so the library is part of HH. ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) keeps a library of guidance that the coding agent reads when it writes the program for a new task, so this library is part of HH as well. VERITAS (Zhang and Shah, 2026) uses a VLM to generate a visual trace and a geometric verifier to score candidate actions during execution. The VLM weights belong to Θ\Theta, whereas the trace representation and geometric scoring logic belong to HH.

A component used only to produce or judge retained changes belongs to Φ\Phi. This covers procedures that run only during improvement, such as the reward code of Eureka (Ma et al., 2024a), the training and algorithm code of ENPIRE (Xiao et al., 2026), and the diagnosis, admission, and search procedures with which ASPIRE builds its library. It also covers learned components that only improvement uses. One kind is the reward model or success detector, as in the reward classifier of MEDAL++ (Sharma et al., 2023a) and the success classifiers of HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2025a) and ConRFT (Chen et al., 2025b). Another is a world model that only serves as the training environment, as in RISE (Yang et al., 2026a), whereas a world model used for planning during task execution belongs to Θ\Theta. Changes to HH and Θ\Theta are capability-level updates. But not every change to a component in Φ\Phi constitutes a meta-level update. During online policy training, critics and reward classifiers may be repeatedly fitted according to a fixed training procedure. Their estimates change as training proceeds, but the procedure itself remains unchanged. These updates are part of running the existing improvement mechanism. A meta-level update changes the mechanism itself, such as its objective, update rule, training configuration, curriculum, or selection criterion, and retains that change for subsequent improvement. Such a change may be implemented in code or learned parameters.

Tasks

A task is what the experimenter asks the robot to accomplish, such as lifting a cup or placing it in the sink. We describe it by two factors. The skill sequence κ\kappa is the sequence of skills required to accomplish the task, such as walking to an object, opening a door, grasping, and pouring. The instance parameters ξ\xi are the variation that leaves κ\kappa unchanged, such as the poses of objects, their arrangement, and the difficulty of a scene as long as the same skills still suffice. This follows the distinction in Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020). Whether the scene is simulated or real is recorded as the source of evidence and does not change the task.

Whether a task has changed depends on its κ\kappa, which can change in two ways (Figure 2(b)). The first is that κ\kappa gains a new skill. Lifting a cup that stands in front of the robot and walking to a table before lifting it are different tasks, because only the second requires navigation. Walking to a table before lifting a cup and walking to a kitchen counter before lifting it are the same task, because both require only navigation and grasping. The second is that κ\kappa is a new combination of skills that the system already has, which is what a long-horizon task usually is. Going from the kitchen to the bedroom and fetching a pair of socks runs navigation, opening the door, and grasping, whereas picking up a piece of clothing in the kitchen and carrying it into the bedroom runs grasping, navigation, and opening the door. The skills are the same but the order differs, so the two are different tasks. This matches the hardest level of GemBench (Garcia et al., 2025), where the robot must compose several skills learned during training.

We apply this distinction to evaluation protocols from seven surveyed systems. Five of these protocols do not establish across-task improvement. HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2025b) trains and tests a policy on USB grasp-insertion, with variation in the initial USB placement. The required skill sequence remains grasping followed by insertion, so only ξ\xi changes. In the pin-insertion experiment considered here, ENPIRE (Xiao et al., 2026) trains and evaluates on the same task. ReWiND (Zhang et al., 2025d) fine-tunes on a task variation new to the pretrained model but evaluates on that same variation. Eureka (Ma et al., 2024a) separately optimizes a reward for each of 29 tasks and evaluates the resulting policy on the corresponding task. In these four cases, improvement and evaluation concern the same κ\kappa. Eurekaverse (Liang et al., 2025) trains on diverse generated parkour courses and evaluates on held-out courses, including combinations of familiar skills. However, the reported protocol does not establish whether the required skill sequences in these test courses were already covered during training. We therefore cannot determine whether the tests change only ξ\xi or also κ\kappa, and conservatively do not treat these results as evidence of across-task improvement. The other two are evaluated across tasks, because κ\kappa changes. ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) constructs its skill library from LIBERO-90 (Liu et al., 2023a), whose tasks are short-horizon, and applies the library zero-shot to held-out long-horizon tasks from LIBERO-Pro Long, which require composing these skills into longer sequences. LRLL (Tziafas and Kasaei, 2024) is tested on unseen compositions of tasks from the current and earlier learning cycles. In both, the test tasks are new combinations of skills the system already has, which is the second way in which κ\kappa can change.

Evaluation scope and evidence sources

A system is scored on the independent evaluator EE of Section 2.1, and which tasks of EE count depends on the claim. A same-task claim is scored on the tasks of EE that have the same κ\kappa as the tasks used for improvement, and an across-task claim on the tasks of EE with a different κ\kappa. An across-task claim also requires that a change retained from improvement on the source tasks is used on the target tasks and contributes to their performance. We write JQσJ_{Q}^{\sigma} for the resulting score under QQ, with σ\sigma either same task or across tasks. Section 6 describes this measurement in detail. For each system, we also record the source of the feedback driving the update and the setting in which the updated system is deployed, each as real, simulated, or imagined.

Levels

We assign a level by four questions. The first is whether Φ\Phi produces a retained change from the system’s own experience. Changes inside a task execution are not improvement (Section 2.2), so a workflow with no such retained change is L0. We also place at L0, as a reference group, workflows whose retained changes depend on people intervening or labeling during improvement, so that L1 to L5 credit only autonomous improvement. The second is what the retained change updates, HH or Θ\Theta at the capability level, or a stage of Φ\Phi at the meta level (Section 2.2). The third is the scope of the gain, which is measured on the same task or across tasks, judged by κ\kappa as above. The fourth is whether the retained changes give a gain, meaning that the final system scores higher than the initial one on JQσJ_{Q}^{\sigma}. A workflow with a gain is placed by its second and third answers, giving L1 to L4 as in Figure 1(b). L5 is an L4 workflow that also shows recursive gain. Starting from the same generation and under the same budget, the system produced by each updated Φk\Phi_{k} scores higher than the one produced by Φk−1\Phi_{k-1}, and the changes it relies on are physically grounded. Figure 3 organizes selected systems by these levels, together with their year, update feedback source, and deployment setting.

3 Harness Adaptation of Physical RSI

The task execution loop connects planning, execution, observation, and correction (Figure. 4). Robot skills and controllers carry out planned actions, while physical feedback informs adjustments to the current behavior or remaining plan. The harness supports this loop through memory, executable skills, and workflows.

Memory supplies decision context through environmental representations and retained experience, as illustrated by object localization in DynaMem (Liu et al., 2025a) and the retrieval of corrective guidance in DROC (Zha et al., 2024). Skills expose robot capabilities through callable programs and interfaces. Code as Policies (Liang et al., 2023) composes perception outputs and control primitives in executable code, while SkiROS2 (Mayr et al., 2023) organizes parameterized skills with explicit execution conditions, exposing program logic, skill parameters, and interfaces as potential modification targets. Workflows govern capability selection and coordination through mechanisms such as feasibility-based selection in SayCan (Ahn et al., 2022) and sequencing and fallback in behavior trees (Colledanchise and Ögren, 2018). Together, these components support adjustments to the current execution, including revised action choices, corrected motion, and updated plans.

The capability improvement loop uses execution feedback and prior modification history to produce persistent updates to memory, skills, and workflows. Feedback interpretation identifies modification targets and scope, guiding the construction of candidate changes. Adopted updates become available for subsequent execution, while attempted changes and their outcomes accumulate as improvement history to inform future updates.

3.1 Feedback Interpretation and Update Target Identification

Execution records and improvement histories support diagnosis by relating observed deviations to the actions, conditions, and previous interventions associated with them. In simulated robot tasks, primitive-level traces in ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026), workflow-node diagnostics in HarnessPAI (Wang et al., 2026c), and visual keyframes in Act-Observe-Rewrite (Kumar, 2026) connect execution outcomes to specific operations and observations. Comparisons across attempts provide additional grounds for interpreting these deviations. In digital agent studies, ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) contrasts successful and failed attempts, while AutoGuide (Fu et al., 2024) relates their differences to the contexts in which corrective guidance applies. Modification histories in WikiSkill (Tang et al., 2026b) and language corrections in DROC (Zha et al., 2024) supplement these comparisons with evidence from previous edits and clarification of task requirements. Together, these sources support hypotheses about the causes of observed failures and the conditions under which they recur.

Selecting a modification target requires determining which harness component should change in response to the diagnosis. When failures concern the use of guidance, AutoManual (Chen et al., 2024) and EmbodiSkill (Ju et al., 2026) distinguish defective instructions from failures to follow valid instructions, directing intervention toward the instructions themselves or reminders of their use. Dynamo (Sun et al., 2026) distinguishes reasoning from perceptual gaps to target textual skills or perception tools. These judgments must then be grounded in editable implementations. HarnessFix (Chen et al., 2026b) links failed trajectory steps to harness code, while RACaP (Li et al., 2026e) identifies interventions involving interfaces, exposed parameters, reporting, routing, or memory. Once the component is identified, the proposal must delimit both the extent of the change and its intended applicability. Self-Harness (Zhang et al., 2026b) favors bounded changes, and SkillAdam (Li et al., 2026a) uses prior editing outcomes to regulate their scope, while RoboFoundry (Liang et al., 2026b) distinguishes task-specific repairs from changes intended for broader reuse. With the diagnosed problem linked to a concrete implementation and a defined scope, the next step is to construct a modification that addresses it within these bounds.

3.2 Memory, Skill, and Workflow Adaptation

Execution memory updates add experiential guidance, organize its application, and revise outdated content (Figure. 5). In digital agent tasks, Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) retains feedback-derived reflections, while ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) extracts reusable insights across attempts. These additions can be organized into context-specific guidance, as in AutoGuide (Fu et al., 2024), or maintained as editable rule collections, as in AutoManual (Chen et al., 2024). Related execution guidance can also be maintained through tool documentation. ContDA (Wu et al., 2026a) revises tool documentation, usage preferences, and fallback guidance as toolsets evolve. In robotics, memory revision additionally concerns the physical explanations underlying action selection. PhysMem (Li et al., 2026b) develops interaction-derived hypotheses and tests their applicability, while KnowBody (Lou et al., 2026) revises action-relevant body relations and rechecks dependent knowledge. Together, these mechanisms update what subsequent execution can draw on and the conditions under which it applies.

Individual capabilities can be updated through changes to their implementation or interface, or supplemented by newly constructed skills and tools. CREATOR (Qian et al., 2023) uses execution errors to guide tool-code correction, while ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) repairs robot task programs using feedback associated with primitive calls. Act-Observe-Rewrite (Kumar, 2026) generates replacement perception and controller code between simulated manipulation trials, changing the computations that interpret observations and produce actions. Other adaptations concern how an existing capability is exposed. RACaP (Li et al., 2026e) includes API and parameter-exposure changes among its candidate modifications. New capabilities can instead be constructed directly or abstracted from task solutions. LATM (Cai et al., 2024) separates tool construction from subsequent invocation, allowing generated functions to serve repeated requests. ViReSkill (Kagaya et al., 2025) stores successful robot plans and control code for later reuse. CRAFT (Yuan et al., 2024a) and SkillWeaver (Zheng et al., 2025) construct parameterized tools and reusable web APIs, respectively, while Playful Agentic Robot Learning (Zhang et al., 2026f) extracts reusable helpers from successful robot programs in simulation. Such changes concern individual capabilities, but shared implementations and callers can require coordinated modification.

Coordinated updates change related capabilities together when they share functionality or depend on common interfaces. ReGAL (Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024) couples the introduction of helper functions with refactoring of the programs that use them, linking library construction to changes in callers. In simulation with human demonstrations and hints, Lifelong Robot Library Learning (Tziafas and Kasaei, 2024) groups robot programs by structural similarity, extracts parameterized skills, and rewrites existing examples to use the resulting library. In both cases, introducing an abstraction is accompanied by changes to existing programs that previously implemented the functionality separately. Coordination also concerns the maintenance of these shared structures. ReGAL edits or prunes abstractions that perform poorly on their associated tests. Playful (Zhang et al., 2026f) extends library-level modification through periodic consolidation of redundant helpers, with dependencies recorded in library entries. The relevant unit of change therefore includes shared functionality and its dependent programs, rather than a collection of independently modified skills.

Execution workflows govern when these capabilities are invoked and how their outputs advance or redirect the task. Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026h) explores staging, action ordering, and invocation timing, retaining successful execution experience to guide later attempts. BATON (Xu et al., 2026a) makes the conditions connecting successive capabilities explicit through invocation, handoff, and lookahead memories. These records guide when a frozen policy can be invoked, what entry state a subsequent subtask requires, and which execution strategy leaves a suitable state for its successor. Changes can also affect the mechanisms that track and advance task progress. RoboFoundry (Liang et al., 2026b) persistently modifies stage processing, active-subgoal construction, and replanning cadence, allowing subsequent executions to use updated procedures for continuing unfinished work. In simulation, RACaP (Li et al., 2026e) evolves its ReAct harness before deployment, then freezes the implementation while retaining observation-dependent action selection, recovery, and stopping decisions. Recovery procedures can likewise be represented as explicit editable rules. In text-agent and simulated object-centric tasks, Kintsugi (Cao et al., 2026) updates policy schemas, monitors, and recovery entries between rollouts. In digital interaction tasks, Living-Harness (Du et al., 2026) converts completed-episode feedback into persistent trigger–recovery records and state-conditioned transitions. Across these representations, updates alter capability invocation, task progression, and recovery in subsequent executions.

3.3 Adoption and Improvement History

Candidate harness updates are checked for their intended effects and their impact on existing capabilities. ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) validates repairs through re-execution, while ReGAL (Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024) uses tests of affected programs to assess changes to shared functions and their callers. These checks inform candidate acceptance, with verification methods discussed further in Section 6.1. Accepted updates become resources available to subsequent execution, including reusable robot plans and control code in ViReSkill (Kagaya et al., 2025) and persistent library helpers in Playful Agentic Robot Learning (Zhang et al., 2026f). Continued execution provides evidence for reassessing adopted resources. In PhysMem (Li et al., 2026b), subsequent interactions strengthen or weaken confidence in retained explanations. In KnowBody (Lou et al., 2026), changes to body estimates prompt renewed checks of dependent rules, linking continued use to the validity of their underlying assumptions. Adoption thus connects candidate updates to subsequent execution, whose feedback informs continued retention, renewed verification, or further modification.

Improvement history links modification attempts to their execution evidence, outcomes, and supporting rationale (Figure 6). ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) records experiments, attempted fixes, skill updates, and observed results, while KnowBody (Lou et al., 2026) preserves original observations and actions alongside outcome assessments, allowing later interpretations to remain traceable to physical evidence. Structured records connect this evidence to specific changes. In digital and simulated tasks, WikiSkill (Tang et al., 2026b) records target skills, edit differences, validation scores, and acceptance decisions, while EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026) accumulates proposals, their rationale, and performance changes, retaining feedback even when candidates are discarded. Across attempts, SkillAdam (Li et al., 2026a) organizes modifications and outcomes by issue, preserving resolution histories and reopening issues when failures recur. Records can also associate update methods with their products, as in MCE (Ye et al., 2026), which stores context-engineering strategies, generated functions, and evaluation metrics together. These practices turn individual attempts into a persistent history for subsequent diagnosis and proposal selection, while making the methods behind those attempts available for further improvement.

3.4 Meta-Improvement of Harness Adaptation

Meta-improvement modifies Adapt\mathrm{Adapt}, the method that generates subsequent harness updates, using evidence accumulated across improvement attempts. Capability improvement can change retained resources and execution procedures under a fixed adaptation method, whereas meta-improvement changes the method itself (Figure 7). Gödel Machines (Schmidhuber, 2006) establish a formal precedent for self-modification, while STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023) and Hyperagents (Zhang et al., 2026e) implement editable improvement procedures in digital systems. For Physical RSI, experiment latency and resource constraints, discussed more broadly in From AGI to ASI (Genewein et al., 2026), motivate improving the quality of updates produced within limited interaction budgets.

Editing experience, difficult cases, and prior evaluations provide different grounds for revising the guidance, resource-construction operations, and programs used by Adapt\mathrm{Adapt}. At the guidance level, SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026d) consolidates editing experience into an optimizer-side meta skill, while Promptbreeder (Fernando et al., 2024) evolves mutation prompts according to the performance of the task prompts they generate. Difficult cases can expose limitations in resource construction, while evaluations of previous designs guide the search for alternatives. MemSkill (Zhang et al., 2026c) uses difficult cases to refine or extend memory-construction skills, MCE (Ye et al., 2026) evolves context-building strategies from previous strategies and evaluations, and ALMA (Xiong et al., 2026) searches designs containing memory-update functions using prior designs and interaction results. These approaches modify the operations constructing retained context or memory rather than merely adding stored content. At the program level, VERSE (Wang et al., 2026f) modifies optimizer-side diagnostic tools and calls to existing checks, while STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023) and Hyperagents (Zhang et al., 2026e) make the update-generating procedure itself editable.

The value of a modified adaptation method depends on the effectiveness and cost of the subsequent updates it produces. STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023) evaluates improvers through the downstream utility of generated programs, while Hyperagents (Zhang et al., 2026e) and SelfSearch (Yang et al., 2026b) use fixed-improver comparisons to examine the contribution of method evolution. Attribution becomes less direct when adaptation methods and runtime components change together, as in MemEvolve (Zhang et al., 2025b) and ALMA (Xiong et al., 2026), and VERSE (Wang et al., 2026f) reports that method evolution does not yield gains in every setting. Evaluation must also distinguish useful improvements from exploitation of the measurement process. Huang et al. (2026) document this risk in digital research tasks, motivating independently checked evidence when evaluating autonomous method changes. For Physical RSI, comparisons under matched initial systems, experience, and budgets should establish whether a candidate method improves later adaptation, with detailed protocols addressed in Section 6.2.

Evaluation outcomes determine whether a candidate method is adopted, revised, or rejected. Adoption requires the changed procedure to govern subsequent improvement attempts. HSI (Zhou, 2026) explicitly executes revised evolution strategies in later rounds, while VERSE (Wang et al., 2026f) conditions optimizer replacement on code checks and a test run, retaining the previous implementation when these checks fail. In Physical RSI, the inherited Adapt\mathrm{Adapt} must produce harness updates that undergo verification and subsequent physical execution. Their outcomes extend the improvement history, providing evidence for retaining the method or targeting further changes to its guidance, operations, or program. This closes the method-level feedback loop, although recursive gains require evidence that successive inherited revisions improve later adaptation, as specified in Definition 2.

4 Model Training of Physical RSI

As illustrated in Figure 1, model learning provides another pathway for improvement alongside adaptation of the model-external harness. Physical experience can support updates to policies, reward models, and world models. A frozen foundation model may assist with failure analysis and training decisions. Figure 8 zooms into this pathway and shows how model learning can form a continuous improvement loop: Physical interaction provides experience for training, and the resulting model updates shape subsequent interactions, forming a feedback loop that may eventually extend to the training procedure itself. This distinction between improving a learnable model and modifying the process that produces future model updates parallels the L0–L5 distinction between task-level improvement and adaptation of the improvement mechanism. Section 6 examines the reliability of the feedback on which both pathways depend.

4.1 Data Preparation

Data preparation couples experience generation with selection for learning. Physical practice prioritizes weak capabilities under scene and reset constraints (Sharma et al., 2023c; Fang et al., 2026b). Simulation generators construct tasks, scenes, rewards, and demonstrations (Wang et al., 2024a; Hua et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024e), expanding coverage and adjusting difficulty to learner performance (Choi et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026). Real2Sim2Real workflows further connect environment preparation to deployment by reconstructing observed scenes in simulation and using the resulting spatial context for physical execution. HomeBody illustrates this route: a foundation-model agent builds a digital twin from robot observations and SLAM geometry to support reasoning and skill execution (Huh et al., 2026). Selection determines how this experience is used. Shared control, active querying, and correction memory provide human guidance (Liu et al., 2023b; Luo et al., 2025a; Hoque et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026a), while recovery demonstrations cover failure states (Ge et al., 2026); dependence on essential human corrective judgments places these workflows at L0. Autonomous selection admits verified successes for imitation and uses failures for value learning or recovery (Zhou et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2026); prioritizing failure-prone states focuses scarce trials on weak behavior (He et al., 2026a). Data preparation contributes to mechanism improvement when a data sampler, curriculum generator, or selection model is revised and reused in subsequent learning (Chebotar et al., 2019; Muratore et al., 2021; Muratore et al., 2022; Sekar et al., 2020).

4.2 Training Methods

Model training typically begins with pretraining on diverse data to establish behavioral, visual, or dynamics priors, followed by post-training with task-specific experience or feedback (Kawaharazuka et al., 2025). Across pretraining and post-training, we review three learning paradigms: imitation learning (IL), self-supervised learning (SSL), and reinforcement learning (RL).

Imitation learning (IL) learns behavior from demonstrations or teacher-generated targets; selected self-generated experience can also supervise later updates (Bousmalis et al., 2023). Behavior cloning can fit continuous actions by regression or predict discrete action tokens autoregressively (Mandlekar et al., 2021a; Kim et al., 2024; Pertsch et al., 2025). Generative imitation instead fits an action distribution: diffusion learns iterative denoising, while flow matching learns a velocity field that transforms noise toward action samples (Chi et al., 2024; Black et al., 2026). Policy distillation instead transfers a teacher’s behavior to a student (Wang et al., 2024f). And adversarial distribution matching provides another route to imitation (Ho and Ermon, 2016). The learning objective can also be the improvement target (Yu et al., 2018), which provides a methodological basis. But evidence of physically grounded, persistent adaptation of IL mechanisms remains limited.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) derives training targets from observations and trajectories by delving into their internal structure and relationships. Reconstruction and latent-action objectives learn visual or motion representations without expert action labels, although mapping them to robot control may require supervised adaptation (Radosavovic et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2025). Predictive learning extends this approach to environmental dynamics (Mendonca et al., 2023). In a physical improvement loop, robot trajectories provide self-supervised targets for updating a predictive model, which then generates imagined experience for subsequent policy training (Wu et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2026a). Self-supervised updates can also adapt policy memory during execution: RoboTTT updates fast weights to incorporate incoming observations into the context used for subsequent actions (Jiang et al., 2026b). At the mechanism level, AutoSSL searches combinations and weights of self-supervised objectives, but does not incorporate a physical robot learning loop (Jin et al., 2022).

Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to improve through repeated interaction: execution outcomes guide policy or value updates, which influence subsequent actions and learning (Hirose et al., 2025; Stachowicz et al., 2025; Mendonca et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026e). Offline data and demonstrations provide a starting point, while online interaction and human corrections support later updates (Nakamoto et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025c; Amin et al., 2025). The learned component may be the base policy or a steering policy around a frozen behavioral prior (Ren et al., 2024; Wagenmaker et al., 2025). In the improvement loop, the reward signal can be adjusted through online reward-model updates or iterative reward-code revision (Zhang et al., 2026g; Huang et al., 2024a). Mechanism-level improvement further targets how learning updates or rewards are generated: DiscoRL learns the rules for updating policies and predictions, while DERL uses policy validation performance to train the meta-optimizer that generates future rewards (Oh et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026).

4.3 Learning Models

The learning methods above apply to diverse models used in robot policies and their training. This section focuses on VLA models, world models, and reward models, which have a strong influence on continual improvement by shaping execution and subsequent learning. VLA updates change actions and collected experience; world-model updates change predictions used for planning or imagined training; reward-model updates change the rewards or value estimates guiding subsequent policy learning.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot commands from visual observations, language instructions, and optional sensory inputs (Kawaharazuka et al., 2025). Continual adaptation incorporates demonstrations, corrective interventions, and deployment trajectories into IL or RL updates (Chen et al., 2025c; Amin et al., 2025). One route updates internal components, including action heads, adapters, backbone layers, or the full model (Kim et al., 2024). Action heads map multimodal representations to discrete tokens or action chunks (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Black et al., 2026); continuous generators include diffusion heads and diffusion Transformers (Ghosh et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b). Updating these components changes action generation, while backbone adaptation can also change visual and instruction grounding. Knowledge Insulation controls this coupling by adapting the backbone through discrete-action supervision while blocking gradients from the continuous-action expert (Driess et al., 2025). Within hierarchical VLAs, internal adaptation may target task interpretation, action generation, or both (Belkhale et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025). A second route keeps a frozen VLA and learns a lightweight controller from physical experience. FIND learns residual corrections using outcome assessment and human assistance for scene recovery (Fang et al., 2026b). RLT instead trains a lightweight actor critic on an RL token from the frozen VLA, refining action chunks while anchoring the actor to VLA recommendations (Xu et al., 2026b). Here, improved behavior is carried by the controller instead of the VLA weights.

World models learn action-conditioned predictions of future observations, latent states, or object relations (Hou et al., 2026a). Robot interaction can adapt predictive priors learned from human video to the deployment environment (Mendonca et al., 2023). Their role in continuing improvement depends on whether these predictions remain fixed or are updated with new experience. A fixed world model can support repeated policy optimization through imagined rollouts (Yang et al., 2026a). Alternatively, new policy rollouts update the world model, which then provides predictions for subsequent policy training (Liu et al., 2026d). The predictor then becomes an evolving source of training experience. Updated predictions can change the actions inferred through inverse dynamics (Du et al., 2023), the ranking of plans or candidate behaviors (Hansen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b), and the synthetic experience used for policy training (Yang et al., 2024). These uses require accurate predictions of action outcomes, beyond visually realistic observations (Guo et al., 2026b). In WAMs, prediction and action generation are integrated within a single model, so world-model adaptation can also affect control (Bi et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026).

Reward models learn to score task progress, success, or relative behavior quality from videos, outcome labels, and trajectory comparisons (Ma et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026a). They support continuing improvement through two distinct paths. A fixed evaluator supplies rewards for successive policy updates, with dense progress estimates complementing sparse task outcomes (Chen et al., 2026e; Fang et al., 2026a; Tan et al., 2025). Alternatively, the evaluator itself learns from new feedback. Reward-model updates can alternate with policy learning, requiring stored experience to be rescored as the learned rewards change (Lee et al., 2021). In physical deployment, reward models can be adapted by human confirmed success used for subsequent policy training (Zhang et al., 2026g). Adaptation to new preferences can be confined to low-rank modules, reducing interference with earlier reward knowledge while keeping the base reward-model weights fixed (Marta et al., 2025). Critic updates provide another form of evaluator adaptation: new successful and failed rollouts refine expected-return estimates used to select actions. This can improve value-guided action selection while the underlying action-generating policy remains frozen (Giridhar et al., 2026).

4.4 Knowledge Transfer and Training Procedure Improvement

Across learning rounds, accumulated knowledge can support new tasks, while feedback from training and execution can inform how subsequent models are trained. We review these routes through cross-task transfer from learned capabilities, followed by feedback-driven improvements to data preparation and training methods.

Cross task transfer uses knowledge acquired on source tasks to support target task learning, while preserving the previously acquired capabilities. Policy initialization starts target task training from a multi-task generalist or a source task policy selected using predicted zero shot success (Bousmalis et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2025). Skill and module reuse instead incorporates learned skill policies or temporal action representations into the target policy, with learning focused on their selection, composition, or adaptation (Zhang et al., 2025c; Zheng et al., 2024a). To adapt these reusable components to a target task, learning can focus on skill selection, expert routing (Wan et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024c), or controller composition (Feng et al., 2025). Throughout updates, replay, modular adaptation, and parameter merging help preserve earlier knowledge while incorporating target-task experience (He et al., 2026b; Yadav et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zhu et al., 2026).

Data preparation improvement uses learning and execution outcomes to revise what experience is prepared for subsequent training. Successful demonstrations do not guarantee robots can reliably learn the demonstrated behaviors. Feedback from policy learning and execution can help identify suitable demonstrations for subsequent training (Chen et al., 2025a; Agia et al., 2025a; Dass et al., 2026). Learning feedback can also guide how data from different sources are mixed for subsequent policy training (Hejna et al., 2024) and informs future experience generation: real-world policy returns guide simulation distributions, while fresh rollouts update predictors that direct collection toward current failure regions (Muratore et al., 2021; He et al., 2026a). These approaches connect data decisions to learner performance. Extending this feedback to autonomous strategy revision, RSIBench-Data evaluates agents that use training and evaluation results to revise data sources, coverage, trajectory representations, and curation strategies in digital tasks (Meng et al., 2026a).

Training method improvement changes training methods for later learning, including revisions to reward code, the training distribution, the update rule, or the organization of training experiments (Ma et al., 2024b; Chebotar et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). Robot rollout results can guide revisions to training code and recipes (Xiao et al., 2026), while records of earlier tuning attempts can guide later training decisions (Li et al., 2026d). These changes enter the self-improvement loop when the system retains and uses them to train subsequent models. Physical RSI additionally requires training-mechanism revisions to be physically grounded: feedback from the robot’s interaction with its environment must inform how the training method changes. Retaining and reusing such a revision can support L2 on the same task or L4 across tasks. L5 further requires showing that the revised mechanism yields better subsequent improvements than its predecessor under matched starting capabilities and resources. Section 6 describes how to test this gain.

5 Safety and Control of Physical RSI

Physical RSI must preserve safety as both the task-execution system M=(Θ,H)M=(\Theta,H) and the improvement procedure Φ\Phi evolve. System updates can change which states the system visits and alter its hazard estimates and action interfaces. Environmental drift can change the dynamics and available control responses. Revisions to Φ\Phi can further change how trials are chosen and updates are accepted, allowing errors in safety assessment to influence later generations.

The reviewed literature mainly provides component results, with limited evidence on safety across inherited revisions of Φ\Phi. Following Section 2.2, safety constrains the execution, capability-level update, and meta-level update loops. Safety requirements and the independent evaluator EE with its scoring criterion QQ remain protected from Φ\Phi even when safeguard implementations change. Under these constraints, control includes restricting actions and trials, specifying permitted operating conditions, and retaining the ability to interrupt execution or improvement. The question throughout this section is which safety evidence remains valid after a change and what must be checked before further physical operation (Figure 9).

5.1 Safe Exploration and Continual Adaptation

Safety during learning.

A policy that is safe after training may still cause harm while collecting experience. Safe reinforcement learning (RL) therefore distinguishes the constrained quantity, the stage at which it is constrained, and the supporting evidence (Gu et al., 2024b; Gu et al., 2023). In a constrained Markov decision process, rewards measure task performance and costs represent safety violations. Constrained Policy Optimization approximately maintains expected-cost limits during policy updates (Achiam et al., 2017). SafeVLA applies constrained learning to unsafe behaviors of vision-language-action models (Zhang et al., 2025a). Other methods address conflicts between reward and safety gradients (Gu et al., 2024a), balance multiple objectives under safety constraints (Gu et al., 2025c), or incorporate risk measures into safety bounds (Gu et al., 2025b). Expected-cost limits can still permit individual violations, and their meaning depends on whether the cost captures the physical hazard.

Retaining safety while adapting.

Safe Continual Domain Adaptation (SCDA) combines safe RL with a penalty on changes to important policy parameters after pretraining across varied simulated conditions (Josifovski et al., 2025). Its robot experiments show adaptation with reduced forgetting and controlled average costs under the tested conditions. The penalty constrains the policy, while learned estimates of reward and safety cost continue adapting. Fitting these estimators to prescribed targets does not by itself establish a meta-level update, even when their parameters persist across rounds (Section 2.3).

Retaining task performance does not necessarily retain safety. In simulated non-stationary benchmarks, Coursey et al. (2026) find that reducing forgetting does not reliably preserve safety performance, while stronger cost penalties can reduce task success. Post-update evaluation should therefore cover both previous and current operating conditions. Historical safety labels should also be reassessed against current dynamics and sensing conditions.

Exploration within a supported region.

Gaussian-process controller optimization restricts quadrotor trials to settings predicted to meet a safety threshold (Berkenkamp et al., 2016). Sequential safe exploration additionally checks reachability and return paths (Turchetta et al., 2016). Stability certificates support joint improvement of a controller and its estimated safe region under regularity and uncertainty assumptions (Berkenkamp et al., 2017).

These results rely on assumptions that may no longer hold after an update to MM or Φ\Phi, or a change in the environment. Before further exploration, the affected cost estimates, uncertainty bounds, and return paths must therefore be checked against current physical conditions. The supported region may need to shrink under drift. If no available trial supports safe continuation under these assumptions, physical exploration must pause.

5.2 Safe Transfer and Update Acceptance

What transfers with a policy.

Transfer of capability does not establish that safety evidence transfers with it. Sim-to-Lab-to-Real combines a learned backup policy with restrictions on unsafe actions and statistical bounds on expected performance and safety (Hsu et al., 2023). Its generalization argument assumes that laboratory and deployment environments follow the same distribution. Robust safe transfer instead uses a guide policy whose tolerance to uncertainty covers the target environment (Zubia et al., 2025). Its expected-cost guarantee requires compatible action spaces and a state mapping that preserves safety conditions.

These assumptions concern the system and environment together. A new encoder can invalidate the state mapping, while an interface change can invalidate the guide’s actions. Neither change necessarily alters the required skill sequence κ\kappa, so safety reassessment also applies within a task as defined in Section 2.3.

Evidence for accepting an update.

Under Sections 2.2 and 6.1, Ver\mathrm{Ver} internally judges changes to MM and to Adapt\mathrm{Adapt} or Train\mathrm{Train}. The independent evaluator EE, using the protected criterion QQ, measures gains in the updated task-execution system and assesses revisions to Ver\mathrm{Ver} by evaluating the systems retained under each verifier. Acceptance determines inheritance. Establishing improvement requires independent outcome evaluation (Section 6.2). Release is the separate authorization for physical operation under specified conditions and safeguards, including restricted trials used to collect evidence.

High Confidence Policy Improvement bounds the probability of accepting a policy below a return threshold (Thomas et al., 2015). The Seldonian framework tests specified behavioral constraints and can return no solution when evidence is insufficient (Thomas et al., 2019). Constrained offline learning and risk-sensitive objectives account for costs and severe outcomes beyond average return (Lee et al., 2022; Chow et al., 2015). Logged data can support policy evaluation and limit policy changes where evidence is sparse (Jiang and Li, 2016; Laroche et al., 2019). The validity of these guarantees and estimates depends on data coverage and estimation assumptions, which must be reconsidered under non-stationarity (Chandak et al., 2020). A gain over an unsafe baseline alone is insufficient.

Releasing a compatible system.

The policy, observation processing, action interface, monitor, and backup controller should be assessed together. Harness changes require checks of skill preconditions, invocation timing, and handover states (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). Changes to execution models require checks of compatibility with the retained harness (Section 4.2). Hardware checks include sensing errors, actuator limits, and control timing. Safety filters can account for bounded sensing errors, as demonstrated by measurement-robust barrier functions in camera-based Segway control (Cosner et al., 2021).

Definitions 1 and 2 allow physical grounding through interaction in a physics simulator or the real world. This grounding condition is distinct from evidence that a particular hardware deployment is safe. Learned world-model predictions can help screen candidates but cannot supply physical grounding on their own. Simulation evidence alone does not establish hardware safety, which requires assessment of the deployed system under its intended physical conditions.

After a system or procedure update, release requires evidence covering the intended conditions and the complete component combination. Improving the score on EE does not supply this evidence by itself. The assessed conditions must remain explicit so that runtime monitoring can detect when they no longer hold.

5.3 Runtime Assurance under Environmental Drift

Preserving a feasible response.

Runtime assurance restricts actions or invokes a backup controller when continued execution threatens safety. Safeguards used during task execution belong to MM: learned model weights are part of Θ\Theta, while filter, switching, and controller code belong to HH. Components used only within the improvement procedure belong to Φ\Phi, while the independent evaluator EE remains outside it (Section 2.1).

Control barrier functions preserve a safe region under model and control-feasibility assumptions (Ames et al., 2017). Action filters can incorporate learned dynamics and uncertainty estimates (Dalal et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2019). Reachability methods account for modeled disturbances (Fisac et al., 2019), while predictive filters check future constraints and safe continuation (Wabersich and Zeilinger, 2021; Tearle et al., 2021). Shielding restricts actions to satisfy logical specifications, including checks that those specifications can be met with the available controls (Alshiekh et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2025). Removing a filter after training removes its direct runtime enforcement (Yang et al., 2026c). Logs must distinguish proposed and executed actions, since frequent corrections can conceal an unsafe policy.

Detecting failure and invalid evidence.

Failure prediction supplies warning signals but does not itself enforce physical constraints. Visual predictors can bound false alarms and missed failures for defined outcomes (Farid et al., 2022). Uncertainty in language-model judgments can support deferring uncertain decisions (Zheng et al., 2024b). Sentinel checks execution consistency and progress (Agia et al., 2025b). SAFE detects task failures from VLA features. Under the exchangeability assumption, its conformal calibration bounds false alarms on successful trajectories, but does not guarantee detection of failures or the safety of intervention (Gu et al., 2025a).

DoReMi and Code-as-Monitor connect execution deviations to replanning or geometric checks (Guo et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a). Other detectors distinguish unusual observations from likely failures (Römer et al., 2025; Rolland et al., 2026). Policy and encoder updates can change both the visited states and the features used by these detectors. Recalibration needs evidence from the updated system. Raising alarm thresholds merely to reduce interventions can conceal declining safety.

Recovery after change.

SOTER and Neural Simplex combine switching rules with backup control (Desai et al., 2019; Phan et al., 2020). Recovery RL learns recovery behavior from estimates of future violations (Thananjeyan et al., 2021). Such methods require a recoverable state and an effective controller. Restoring an earlier policy cannot reverse a mechanical fault or changed friction. Learned resetting and return behaviors support autonomous practice but also require physical trials and can fail (Eysenbach et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023b). In shared workspaces, coordinated control must remain feasible when other robots change their behavior (Wang et al., 2017).

Changes to a policy, monitor, or backup controller require joint checks of detection errors, response delays, and recovery feasibility. Revisions to Φ\Phi must carry these checks into subsequent updates. Monitoring must track the physical assumptions as well as task failures, and restrictions must act before recovery becomes infeasible. Abrupt changes outside the assumed disturbance bounds remain outside the guarantee.

5.4 Oversight of an Evolving Improvement Procedure

Constraining how successors are produced.

Changes to Adapt\mathrm{Adapt}, Train\mathrm{Train}, or Ver\mathrm{Ver} affect the trials used to develop later systems and the decisions that retain them. Omitting intervention records from DD can make assisted task success appear to show that a policy is safe on its own. Procedure assessment must therefore include the physical trials and subsequent systems it produces, rather than only the final policy’s performance.

Formal guarantees cover some structured updates. Fulton and Platzer (2019) revise models, control logic, and associated proofs, then eliminate inconsistent models during operation. Their safety result requires an accurate model to remain in the candidate set. This supports the specified model and controller updates, not arbitrary revisions of Φ\Phi.

Preserving requirements and evaluation.

A revised cost estimator must still measure the hazards specified by the protected requirements. If one learned model both proposes actions and assesses their safety, shared prediction errors can affect both decisions. A verifier can also drift toward accepting updates that pass its local checks while increasing physical risk. Changes to Ver\mathrm{Ver} therefore require assessment through protected E,QE,Q and evidence from the systems retained under the competing verifier versions (Section 6.1). The safety criteria for accepting a revision of Ver\mathrm{Ver} should be specified before testing and protected from modification by the candidate verifier. Passing these safety checks does not by itself establish downstream recursive gain, which requires the controlled comparisons of Section 6.2.

Instructions embedded in external content can redirect an agent (Greshake et al., 2023). When Φ\Phi reads logs or edits code, this content must not acquire permission to change protected requirements or disable stopping mechanisms.

Human control and autonomous inheritance.

Human demonstrations and corrections may enter DD under the system description in Section 2.1. Their use must nevertheless be distinguished from the autonomy required for a level claim. Section 2.3 assigns workflows whose retained changes depend on human intervention or labeling during improvement to L0. Direct human edits to Θ\Theta, HH, or Φ\Phi also violate the self-inheritance condition, and human selection of retained updates replaces autonomous retention. Authorization for physical operation is a separate safety decision. Its role, and any interventions that contribute to learning or update selection, must be recorded explicitly (Section 6.2).

Human interventions provide experience for policy learning (Kelly et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023b; Luo et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025b), although uncertain or suboptimal guidance needs additional care (Zhao et al., 2025). Emergency stops should remain distinguishable from demonstrations of successful behavior. Methods for allocating human attention and requesting clarification can reduce supervision demands (Hoque et al., 2022; Hoque et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2023), but do not ensure help arrives before danger. AutoRT and SOP provide supervision and intervention infrastructure (Ahn et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2026). Work on interruptible learning and the Off-Switch Game addresses incentives around interruption (Orseau and Armstrong, 2016; Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017). Physical intervention also depends on sensing, communication, actuation, and response time.

Before inheriting a revision of Φ\Phi, assessment must check how it changes trial selection, interpretation of interventions, and update acceptance. Protected requirements and effective stopping mechanisms must persist through the change.
