Replacing a safeguard additionally requires compatible controllers and a recoverable physical state at handover. Human involvement in operational safety and in inheritance decisions must be recorded separately.

5.5 Safety Evidence across Generations

Each generation needs records linking its system and procedure versions to the physical conditions, interventions, and outcomes behind its safety assessment. These records allow later changes to be checked against the assumptions on which earlier decisions relied. Table 3 summarizes the evidence available for different changes and the checks needed before reuse.

Risk across rounds.

A bound for one round does not establish a lifetime guarantee. If VkV_{k} denotes a physical violation in round kk and valid bounds Pr⁡(Vk)≤δk\Pr(V_{k})\leq\delta_{k} hold for the adaptive process, then

Pr⁡(⋃k=1KVk)≤∑k=1Kδk.\Pr\!\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}V_{k}\right)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{k}.

This union bound needs no independence, but its per-round bounds must remain valid for the adaptive process. Estimates from obsolete models cannot supply them. Physical risk accumulates during rejected trials, recovery, and resetting, while hardware wear can alter the assumptions used in later assessments. Risk incurred while developing a revision of Φ\Phi should be recorded separately from risk during its subsequent use, alongside the resource accounting discussed in Section 6.2.

False acceptance of an update is distinct from physical harm. Repeated selection needs statistical error control, and adaptive reuse of test feedback requires fresh evidence or a correction for the resulting dependence (Dwork et al., 2015). In the architecture of Section 2.2, judgments from Ver\mathrm{Ver} or EE are recorded in DD. If external judgments influence later proposals or candidate acceptance, the associated evidence cannot also serve as untouched final evaluation. Records must distinguish feedback used during improvement from evidence reserved for independent assessment (Section 6.2). Protecting evaluation tasks and QQ from direct access or modification does not by itself remove adaptive selection effects.

Evaluation after change.

Safety evaluation should cover adaptation, rejected trials, resets, and recovery, reporting violation frequency and severity, near misses, missed failures, intervention delays, and recovery success. Tests immediately after updates reveal failures hidden by final-policy averages. Revisiting previous conditions tests safety retention. Comparing fixed and updated systems under both stable and drifting conditions helps distinguish environmental effects from update effects.

Safe operation and recursive gain require distinct evidence. For L5, each assessed revision of Φ\Phi must be autonomously inherited and produce better subsequent improvements across tasks than its predecessor. The matched comparison and independent evaluation requirements are specified in Definition 2 and Section 6.2.

For safety, these comparisons must also match safety rules, stopping and reset conditions, and the arrangements for human oversight and authorization for physical operation. Actual interventions and deviations from these conditions must be recorded, together with risk incurred during adaptation and recovery. Repeated trials under matched operating conditions help account for physical variability.

Safety evidence can be reused only while the relevant assumptions and statistical bounds remain valid. Each inherited change must therefore be linked to checks of the affected safeguards and to the physical risk incurred in producing and using it. These checks support assessment under stated conditions, not a guarantee for arbitrary environmental drift or unrestricted Physical RSI.

6 Verification and Evaluation of Physical RSI

Evaluating Physical RSI requires assessing both whether candidate updates pass verification and whether their subsequent use improves task performance or the improvement procedure. Following Section 2.1, verification within the improvement procedure Φ\Phi examines whether proposed updates should be accepted and inherited, while independent evaluation uses an external EE and criterion QQ to assess the updated task-execution system M=(Θ,H)M=(\Theta,H). Passing internal verification does not by itself establish subsequent improvement, which requires independent evaluation. As illustrated in Figure 10, this section reviews verification practices for candidate updates (Section 6.1), evaluation of improvement outcomes (Section 6.2), and related benchmarks (Section 6.3).

6.1 Verification of Candidate Updates

Verification checks whether a candidate update is ready for adoption by examining its implementation, its effect on the target problem, and its impact on existing capabilities. Following Section 2.1, Ver\mathrm{Ver} is part of the improvement procedure Φ=(Adapt,Train,Ver)\Phi=(\mathrm{Adapt},\mathrm{Train},\mathrm{Ver}) and informs which updates to M=(Θ,H)M=(\Theta,H) or to the improvement procedure are accepted and inherited. These internal checks use development evidence, instead of replacing the protected external evaluation EE under criterion QQ.

Implementation Validity. Implementation checks examine whether a candidate can run correctly within the system, including syntax, interfaces, formats, and execution outputs. Checks at stage boundaries or before task execution identify implementation errors before more costly task tests, as illustrated by HARBOR and HarnessPAI (Li et al., 2026d; Wang et al., 2026c). Passing these checks establishes that the candidate can be tested; its task effect still requires execution evidence.

Repair Effectiveness. Repair checks assess whether a modification resolves the targeted problem. Re-execution on failed cases and comparison with preceding versions on matched task instances provide evidence through outcomes and execution traces (Lu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026). These tests connect the proposed correction to its measured effect within tested conditions. Applying an update to other tasks requires evidence of its effectiveness beyond the original case: RoboFoundry checks general updates by generating repair proposals from other pre-repair records and assessing them against previously successful repair updates and their execution outcomes (Liang et al., 2026b).

Capability Preservation. Preservation checks revisit successful tasks or conditions to detect losses caused by a shared modification. Acceptance criteria may require previously successful tasks to remain successful or restrict performance losses on individual tasks. RPG and HarnessPAI retest the updated systems before accepting changes to check that previously successful tasks remain successful (Wang et al., 2026d; Wang et al., 2026c). Preserving existing capabilities also requires checking whether previously learned knowledge remains valid after an update: KnowBody suspends rules that depend on revised body estimates until they are revalidated (Lou et al., 2026).

Meta-verification. When Ver\mathrm{Ver} itself is revised, its acceptance rules become part of the object under examination. This evaluation matters because verification mechanisms used to assess candidate updates can themselves make incorrect judgments, as documented by FailBench and No Free Checker (Navasardyan et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026). VERSE provides a digital example of developing verification-related tools around fixed checking primitives (Wang et al., 2026f). Such revisions cannot be judged solely by their own acceptance standards: accepting more updates does not establish that a revised verifier is better. Independent evaluation should therefore compare the subsequent performance of systems produced under the original and revised verification procedures, using a common external evaluation set EE and scoring criterion QQ.

6.2 Evaluation of Improvement Outcomes

Whereas verification determines which candidate updates are accepted, independent evaluation uses the protected evaluator EE and scoring criterion QQ (Section 2.1) to assess the effects of changes retained in later task-execution systems M=(Θ,H)M=(\Theta,H). Revisions to the improvement procedure Φ\Phi are assessed indirectly through the subsequent systems they produce. We review how existing studies assess performance across improvement rounds, identify the contributions and transferability of updates, and report resource costs and human involvement.

Performance and Retention. Existing evaluations examine both the gains from a single learning update and how performance evolves across successive improvement rounds. Before–after comparisons measure changes in task success (Zhou et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026). Multi-round evaluations extend this comparison to successive policy checkpoints or updated agent systems, tracking whether gains accumulate, persist, or temporarily decline (Lang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d). To assess these changes independently, updated systems are evaluated under initial conditions that were not used for debugging or selecting candidate updates (Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d).

Attribution and Transfer. Controlled comparisons identify which changes contribute to improvement, while transfer tests examine their usefulness beyond single tasks. EmbodiRSI compares adaptive and static collection with matched trajectory counts, initial data, policy architectures, and training recipes (Lang et al., 2026). RPG ablates diagnostic inputs and separately compares skill-library versions with the runtime model, prompt, perception, and execution budgets fixed (Wang et al., 2026d). ASPIRE evaluates library snapshots accumulated from different numbers of source tasks, including an empty-library baseline on unseen tasks; it also tests simulation-discovered skills on a different physical embodiment (Lu et al., 2026). These evaluations connect gains to specific changes and assess whether their benefits can be reused beyond the original tasks and embodiments.

Efficiency and Autonomy. Several studies report the resources behind improvement and distinguish autonomous execution from assistance during development. ENPIRE measures robot and GPU utilization, token consumption, and time and tokens needed to reach success, exposing trade-offs between faster improvement and resource efficiency (Xiao et al., 2026). KnowBody reports planner rounds alongside task completion and tracks decision effort during continual interaction (Lou et al., 2026). F4R compares methods under matched data-preparation time budgets and itemizes reconstruction, collection, and training costs (Yu et al., 2026). Autonomy is assessed through explicit execution conditions: EmbodiRSI disables human correction and agent takeover during policy evaluation, while RPG distinguishes autonomous practice updates from human setup and hardware adaptation, then evaluates frozen physical systems without human assistance (Lang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d). These reports relate improvements to resource use and human involvement.

6.3 Benchmarks and Evaluation Resources

Table 4 organizes existing resources into embodied and RSI-related benchmarks according to their primary evaluation focus. The resources include task suites, benchmark protocols, and supporting evaluation frameworks; a resource may support more than one focus.

Embodied benchmarks. Task-oriented benchmarks assess task learning, performance, and generalization (Liu et al., 2023a), as well as robustness and physical-world performance (Zhou and others, 2025; Atreya et al., 2025). Alongside task-level evaluations, supporting resources examine the reliability of success and reward judgments (Navasardyan et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026) and world-model-based policy assessment (Tseng et al., 2026). Evaluation also extends to the development process, assessing robot programming and policy-training workflows (Fu et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026).

RSI-related benchmarks (primarily digital). Recent resources examine agent-driven method development and iterative improvement in digital settings. AI4AI-Bench and RSIBench-Data assess changes to training algorithms and data strategies through subsequent model performance (Chi et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026a). RSI-Exam and HarnessDev evaluate executable method or harness revisions (RSI-Exam Team, 2026; Wu et al., 2026c), while PAST-Bench examines the contribution of accumulated experience to later agent performance (Xue et al., 2026). However, a benchmark jointly evaluating the Physical RSI methods remains an open need.

7 Challenges and Future Directions

Learning from uncertain physical experience. Physical interaction provides data and learning signals for robot training, but partial observability, sensor noise, and stochastic outcomes make it difficult to distinguish informative feedback from misleading signals. In Physical RSI, when the system uses uncertain feedback to revise its own training procedure, it may carry misguided updates into later rounds and repeatedly reinforce them through subsequent learning. How to derive reliable learning signals from physical experience so that inherited procedure changes improve subsequent learning without compounding feedback errors remains an open challenge.

Causal attribution across harness components.

Execution feedback does not uniquely identify the harness components responsible for failure. Dependencies among memory, skills, and workflows allow errors to propagate, so observed deviations may reflect upstream defects or interactions among otherwise valid components. Concurrent updates further confound attribution, as performance changes cannot be assigned to individual modifications without controlled comparisons. Partial observability and limited physical trial budgets restrict such comparisons, leaving both the source of failure and the effect of intervention uncertain. Effective harness adaptation therefore depends on distinguishing causal dependencies from observed associations and isolating the effects of modifications sufficiently to justify their targets and scope.

Non-stationarity in the improvement loop.

Evidence supporting a retained update is conditional on the system configuration and physical conditions under which it was obtained. Subsequent component revisions can alter dependencies and invalidate compatibility assumptions, while environmental changes can shift the conditions governing an update’s effectiveness. Historical outcomes consequently provide uneven support for current adoption decisions. The same dependence applies to improvement strategies, whose measured effectiveness may change with the capabilities and experience available to the system. Sustained improvement requires tracking these dependencies and reassessing evidence as its underlying conditions change, while limiting the physical cost of revalidation.

Reward hacking and evaluation leakage.

Improvement procedures in Physical RSI rely on success detectors, learned rewards, and model-based judgments that may not faithfully reflect physical task outcomes. Benchmarks of robotic outcome assessment expose errors in these signals (Navasardyan et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026), while reward hacking in digital research agents illustrates how optimization can exploit an imperfect evaluation target (Huang et al., 2026). As Φ\Phi evolves, changes to Train\mathrm{Train} or Ver\mathrm{Ver} may amplify such biases across subsequent updates. Moreover, even when the external evaluator EE and criterion QQ are protected from direct access, repeated use of evaluation results for candidate selection can compromise their statistical independence (Dwork et al., 2015). A central direction is therefore to combine independently checked physical outcomes with controlled disclosure of evaluation feedback and fresh or statistically corrected final tests, so that higher scores reflect actual capability gains rather than exploitation of the measurement process.

Safety across recursive updates.

Maintaining safety becomes harder as Φ\Phi evolves, particularly when drift in Ver\mathrm{Ver} favors updates that pass local checks while increasing physical risk. Existing guarantees remain limited: the proof-preserving methods reviewed in Section 5 cover structured model and controller revisions (Fulton and Platzer, 2019). Extending these guarantees to inherited changes in Φ\Phi remains open. Exhaustive revalidation after every update can exceed physical trial budgets and itself incur harm. A concrete direction is selective reassessment: identifying assumptions invalidated by an update or environmental drift, reusing evidence that remains valid, and concentrating new trials on unresolved safety claims. Such reassessment requires per-round risk bounds to remain valid as verification and data collection adapt, while preserving protected requirements and effective interruption. Comparisons of successive procedures from matched starting systems and experience, under equal budgets, fixed safety rules, and protected E,QE,Q, would test whether recursive gain can be established across tasks without relaxing constraints or concealing physical risk incurred during rejected trials, resets, and recovery.

Benchmarking verified recursive gain.

Existing robot benchmarks assess task performance, feedback reliability, and agent-driven program or training development (Navasardyan et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026), but do not directly establish whether revisions to the improvement procedure Φ\Phi make subsequent improvement more effective. Higher successor performance may result from accumulated experience or stronger starting systems rather than a better improvement mechanism. The central challenge is to evaluate mechanism-level recursive gain under comparable conditions. Future benchmarks should track autonomous revisions, inheritance, and subsequent use of Φ\Phi, and compare Φk\Phi_{k} with Φk−1\Phi_{k-1} from the same starting generation and experience, under matched tasks and resource budgets.

8 Conclusion

This study introduces a unified framework for Physical Recursive Self-Improvement, extending robot autonomy from task execution to improving both capabilities and the procedures that produce them. The L0–L5 framework classifies systems according to their update targets, task scope, and evidence of recursive gain. Guided by this framework, we investigate existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside the safety, control, and evaluation mechanisms that support successive updates. Our analysis highlights a key gap: improved task performance alone does not establish that the improvement procedure itself has become more effective. Demonstrating Physical RSI therefore requires independent comparisons of successive procedures under matched starting conditions and resource budgets, with gains demonstrated across tasks. Future progress depends on reliable physical feedback, clearer attribution of gains to procedure changes, and safety assessments that remain valid as systems and environments evolve. Addressing these challenges would pave the way for robots that autonomously improve both what they can do and how they learn, while ensuring safety. The ultimate goal of Physical RSI is for robots to become increasingly capable of improving themselves as they encounter new tasks and challenges in the physical world.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
